subject: Culture
title: Alphabet Revolutions
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Alphabet Revolutions.

hook.text: In 1928 Turkey switched from Arabic to Latin script overnight. Millions became illiterate in their own language.

buildup.text: Atatürk believed Arabic script tied Turkey to a past he wanted to erase. Latin script meant modernization.

discovery.text: Korea's King Sejong invented Hangul in 1443 so commoners could read. Nobles fought it for centuries.

twist.text: Vietnam switched from Chinese characters to Latin-based quốc ngữ under French rule—colonialism reshaped thought.

climax.text: Every script change rewires who can access knowledge and who is locked out.

punchline.text: Change the alphabet and you change who has power.

quiz.question: Who invented the Korean Hangul script?

details.summary: Alphabet changes are political revolutions. Turkey switched from Arabic to Latin script in 1928 to Westernize. Kazakhstan is shifting from Cyrillic to Latin to distance itself from Russia. Korea's King Sejong invented hangul to democratize literacy away from Chinese characters.
details.whyItMatters: Alphabet revolutions demonstrate that writing systems are political instruments, not neutral technologies. Changing a script is changing a civilization's orientation and identity.
takeaways: Atatürk's 1928 alphabet switch severed Turkey from Ottoman texts overnight
King Sejong invented hangul so commoners could read and write
Kazakhstan began switching from Cyrillic to Latin alphabet in 2017

faq.question: Why did Turkey change its alphabet?
faq.answer: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk replaced the Arabic script with the Latin alphabet in 1928 as part of his broader Westernization campaign. The change was implemented in months — the entire population had to learn a new writing system.

faq.question: Why did Korea need a new alphabet?
faq.answer: Before hangul (created 1443), Koreans used Chinese characters that took years to master, restricting literacy to the elite. King Sejong designed hangul to be learnable in a single day, explicitly to empower commoners.
